summary: Defines a way for IKEv2 implementations to tell peers which authentication methods they support while setting up Security Associations. This helps when a peer has several credentials of different types.

plainLanguage.summary: Before two people exchange secrets, they say which kinds of ID each can accept. This lets VPN software announce that, avoiding failed attempts.

questions: how do ikev2 peers announce authentication methods
subtitle: How IKEv2 peers tell each other which authentication methods they support, before they pick one.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 has no way to negotiate an authentication method. A peer that holds several credentials, or can make several kinds of signature, may pick a method the other side does not support, and the SA setup fails.
tldr.mechanism: A new SUPPORTED_AUTH_METHODS notification carries an ordered list of announcements. The responder sends it in IKE_SA_INIT (or later in IKE_INTERMEDIATE), the initiator sends it in IKE_AUTH, and each side may use the list when choosing how to authenticate.
tldr.outcome: Sending and using the list is optional for both sides, so peers that do not know the extension simply ignore it. RFC 9593 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9593 is a Proposed Standard, published in July 2024. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem With Guessing
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2, RFC 7296) sets up keys for IPsec. Unlike IKEv1 (RFC 2409), it does not negotiate how the peers authenticate. Each peer simply picks whatever method it thinks fits the credentials it has.

That works when the choice is obvious. It breaks when one peer has several credentials of different types and the other supports only some of them. It also breaks when one credential can produce different kinds of authentication tokens, such as signatures in different formats. IKEv2 requires each peer to use exactly one method and gives no way to say which ones it supports, so the more capable peer can choose a method the other cannot handle.

The RFC also notes that emerging post-quantum signature algorithms, especially hybrid schemes, may make this harder.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine one kid has a library card, a school ID and a passport, but the club only accepts the school ID. Without being told, the kid might pick the wrong one and get turned away.

sections.title: Where the List Is Sent
sections.content:
Each party may send its peer a list of the authentication methods it supports and is configured to use. The list travels in a new Notify payload of type SUPPORTED_AUTH_METHODS. The sender may also mark some methods as usable only with particular trust anchors. The receiver may use this when it has several ways to compute its AUTH payload.

The responder sends its list, ordered by preference, in the IKE_SA_INIT response if it is willing to use the extension. The initiator sends its own ordered list in the IKE_AUTH request, whether or not it received the responder's list. An initiator that does not know the extension ignores the notification as an unknown status notify.

The list in IKE_SA_INIT could make the response large enough for IP fragmentation. If the list is large and both peers support the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange (RFC 9242), the responder MAY send an empty notification in IKE_SA_INIT and deliver the real list later. IKE fragmentation (RFC 7383) can then handle the long message.

On seeing the empty notification, the initiator MAY start an IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange just for this purpose. It MAY include its IDi (and possibly IDr) payloads so the responder can send only the methods that fit that initiator. Those payloads MUST match the ones later sent in IKE_AUTH. If several IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges happen, the responder is RECOMMENDED to use the last one.

If several SUPPORTED_AUTH_METHODS notifications appear in one message, together they form a single ordered list, unless another extension overrides that.
sections.plainLanguage: The host says first which IDs it takes. If the list is very long, the host says 'ask me again in a minute' and sends the long list later, so it does not get squashed on the way.

sections.title: The Notify Payload and Announcements
sections.content:
The payload is a standard IKEv2 Notify payload (RFC 7296, Section 3.10) with Protocol ID set to 0, SPI Size set to 0 and Notify Message Type set to 16443. The notification data is a list of announcements. Each one is a variable-size blob that starts with a length octet, then an octet holding the authentication method from the IANA "IKEv2 Authentication Method" registry. Implementations MUST ignore announcements whose semantics they do not understand.

There are three formats:

  • 2-octet: for methods not based on public key cryptography, namely "Shared Key Message Integrity Code" (2) and "NULL Authentication" (13).
  • 3-octet: for public key methods, adding a Cert Link octet. The older RSA (1), DSS (3) and ECDSA (9, 10, 11) methods use it, though they are superseded by "Digital Signature" (14).
  • Multi-octet: for "Digital Signature" (14), with an ASN.1 AlgorithmIdentifier in DER after the Cert Link octet. This is the method from RFC 7427.

A non-zero Cert Link value N means the method is meant only for the N-th CA in the CERTREQ payload(s) sent by that peer. Zero means any CA. If no CERTREQ was received, the field MUST be ignored and treated as zero. To make this linking easy, the notification is always in the same message as the CERTREQ payload.
sections.plainLanguage: Each item on the list is a small label saying which ID type is accepted, and sometimes which office is allowed to issue it. A zero means any office will do.

sections.title: Interaction With Other IKEv2 Extensions
sections.content:
Normally each IKEv2 party chooses its own authentication method independently. Some extensions break that rule, and the RFC says how to deal with them.

With the Secure Password Framework (RFC 6467), the peers negotiate one password method in IKE_SA_INIT and both use it, so there is nothing to announce. If they choose secure password authentication, they MUST NOT send SUPPORTED_AUTH_METHODS. For the same reason, the Generic Secure Password method (12) has no 2-octet announcement.

With Multiple Authentication Exchanges (RFC 4739), peers MAY send several SUPPORTED_AUTH_METHODS notifications, one per authentication round, in the order they prefer to perform the rounds.
sections.plainLanguage: If both kids already agreed to use one special password game, they do not need to list their IDs. If there are several checkpoints, they can give a list for each one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Announcing methods gives an eavesdropper extra information about what the peers support. Security properties of each method are described in the documents listed in the IANA registry.

An active on-path attacker can strip announcements. If a peer advertises "NULL Authentication" with other methods, removing the rest can push the peers toward NULL authentication. The RFC says this is not a real downgrade attack, because IKEv2 does not negotiate authentication methods and local policy should allow NULL authentication in that case.

Likewise, if an attacker can break some announced methods online, removing the other announcements may lead the peers to use a weaker one, and a successful attack could then become a person-in-the-middle attack.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person in the middle could rip names off the list so only the weakest ID is left. So a peer should only list IDs it is happy to use.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Appendix A is informative and gives two scenarios. In the first, the list fits in IKE_SA_INIT, so no IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange is needed. The responder announces the Shared Key Message Integrity Code and NULL Authentication methods, and the initiator answers that it supports only the shared key method.

In the second, the responder announces "Digital Signature" with RSASSA-PSS for CA1 and CA2 and with ECDSA for CA3. It sends an empty notification in IKE_SA_INIT and the real list in IKE_INTERMEDIATE, along with its CERTREQ payloads. The initiator supports only RSASSA-PSS with no CA link.
sections.plainLanguage: In one example the list is short and goes in the first message. In the other it is long, so it waits for a second message.

messages.label: IKE_SA_INIT response
messages.note: CERTREQ and an empty SUPPORTED_AUTH_METHODS notification.

messages.label: IKE_INTERMEDIATE response
messages.note: CERTREQ and the full list of announcements.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the blob in octets; must be 3.

fields.name: Cert Link
fields.desc: Links the announcement to the N-th CA in the CERTREQ; zero means any CA.
